# Theory and Hypotheses

<br>

Over time, the theoretical model has been extended to include all out-group members (bron), and even members of other out-groups that were not directly involved in the contact at all. The latter is known as a secondary transfer effect of intergroup contact (Pettigrew, 2009), and has been studied extensively. This secondary transfer effect seems to be conditional; only when the secondary out-group is similar in culture, stigma, or status (= generalization gradient effect).

Additionally, growing bodies of research study indirect contact (**extended**=simply knowing an in-group member has out-group friend, Zhou et al., 2018; **vicarious**=observing other in-group members, online, reading stories) - see Tropp et al., 2022; Stark et al., 2025. Experimental research even shows support for secondary transfer effects when contact with the primary group was merely observed in others or even imagined (Harwood et al., 2011; Vezzali et al., 2014).

Secondary transfer effects are not always found → social influence can help explain this; who influences who? (is it all kinds of friends, or just in- or out-group friends?) “Some studies reported social influence from ingroup but not from outgroup friends (Bracegirdle et al., 2023), implying that having outgroup friends is not associated with outgroup attitudes. Others found influence of outgroup friends’ attitudes on generalized prejudice (Zingora & Flache, 2025).” Most recent research shows → people’s attitudes to secondary outgroups changed not due to having friends from the primary outgroup but due to the attitudes that those primary outgroup friends hold toward secondary outgroups **!!!**

research exists that combines intergroup contact theory (secondary transfer effects) and social network analysis (see bronnen). Results from social network analysis on extended contact support this idea: extended contact reduces prejudice only when some of the outgroup friends of one’s ingroup friends are known. So: only in mixed triads, not in open triads (Stark, 2019).

Recent studies say: it’s actually fully influence, not transfer. “Friendships with primary outgroup members may have negative implications for secondary outgroups when those friends hold more negative attitudes” (Zingora et al., 2026). Having outgroup friends was not linked to more positive intergroup attitudes once social influence (i.e., ingroup friends’ attitudes) was accounted for (for a meta-analysis, see Zingora, 2025). The importance of social influence is further demonstrated by Bracegirdle et al. 2026: “Socialization was strongest among friends who held initially opposing attitudes, which led both high- and low-prejudice individuals to become more neutral over time. The findings thus suggest that socialization has a neutralizing effect, rather than a polarizing effect”. Big conclusion = Friends’ out-group attitudes become more similar to each other. If the friends are negative: you will become more negative (and vice versa).

<br>

## Hypotheses

1.  **Classic STE** -\> Egos with more female friends (*primary outgroup*) in T1 are more likely to be friends with ethnic minority students (*secondary outgroup*) in T2

    [Students prefer / students with lower levels of X]{.underline}

    -   But what is the effect?

    1.  This effect is mediated by ego's tolerance (comfy with ethnic minorities)
    2.  This effect is stronger when egos friends are tolerant (comfy with ethnic minorities) -\> **Influence effect?**
    3.  This effect is stronger when ego is ethnic majority and/or male

<br>

1.  **Influence** -\> Egos with more tolerant friends (whose friends are comfy with ethnic minorities; *secondary outgroup attitudes*) are more likely to be friends with ethnic minority students (*secondary outgroup*) in T2
    1.  This effect is mediated by ego's tolerance (comfy with ethnic minorities)
    2.  This effect is stronger when egos friends are female -\> **Secondary transfer effect?**
    3.  This effect is stronger when ego is ethnic majority and/or male

<br>
